title: Sitting between
hookLine: a short sitting between prostrations, asking forgiveness

cards: The second after a door shuts. The breath between two sentences in a hard conversation. The red light before it turns green.
Small pauses, usually rushed through or filled with a phone. In the prayer, one of these tiny pauses is built in on purpose. The forehead comes up from the floor.
The person sits back on their heels, and for a few seconds, before going down again, sits still and says something short. It would be easy to skip. The Prophet ﷺ never did.

teach.b: The sitting is often called jalsa, just a sitting, from the everyday word for sitting down.

Every unit of prayer has two prostrations, and between them the person rises with Allahu akbar and sits, usually on the left foot with the right foot upright, hands resting on the thighs. What do they say?
A hadith in the Sunan, from the companion Hudhayfah, reports the Prophet saying here: rabbi ighfir li, rabbi ighfir li.
My Lord, forgive me. My Lord, forgive me. That's it.
Another report, from Ibn Abbas, gives a longer line, asking God to forgive, to have mercy, to guide, to give well-being, and to provide: five things in one breath.
Either one is said quietly, then Allahu akbar, and back down to the floor. Now the surprise. You'd think such a short moment would be hurried.

teach.h: SO LONG THEY THOUGHT HE'D FORGOTTEN.
teach.b: A companion named Anas, in Bukhari, said the Prophet would sit between the two prostrations so long that someone would say, he's forgotten. He hadn't. He was just staying there.
The hadith of the man who prayed too fast, met twice already on this path, includes this too: sit until you're at rest in your sitting. So the pause isn't empty space between two important things.
It's its own small place. Down to the floor, closest to God; up, sitting, and the first thing said is forgive me; then down again.
A rhythm like breathing: low, a breath between, low again.

how: Between the two prostrations of each unit, Muslims sit briefly and still, commonly saying rabbi ighfir li, my Lord, forgive me, or a longer supplication for mercy, guidance, well-being and provision.

o: the short sitting between the two prostrations
a short nap after the midday meal
a rest you take once the prayer is over

games.q: what's inside the sitting — tap the pairs.

s: the sitting between prostrations is a quick pass-through
the hadith says sit until you're at rest; Anas said the Prophet ﷺ sometimes sat so long people thought he'd forgotten.
the words in the sitting ask for forgiveness
rabbi ighfir li: my Lord, forgive me (reported from Hudhayfah).
there's only one prostration in each unit
there are two, with this sitting between them.

games.q: you're praying behind the Prophet ﷺ. he's sitting between the prostrations, and the pause keeps going. what's happening?
o: he's staying in the sitting, unhurried
games.why: Anas said he'd sit so long someone would say he'd forgotten. he hadn't; the sitting was its own place (Bukhari).

practice: Sit back, on your heels if that's comfortable, or in a chair with your hands resting on your thighs, and let one breath come in and go out.

If you pray, say it once, quietly: rabbi ighfir li, my Lord, forgive me; if you don't, think of one thing you'd like to be let off for, and hold it lightly. Then stay seated, and let the pause be long.

wordCard.voice: Jalsa. The short sitting between the two prostrations, where the words are: my Lord, forgive me. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: my Lord, forgive me, the words said in the sitting between the prostrations.

carryVoice: Your line: a breath between. Even the shortest pause in the prayer has its own words. Day one hundred six.
